title: A Practical Guide to Efficient AI: Shelby Heinecke
talk_summary: Shelby Heinecke (Salesforce) lays out five dimensions of AI efficiency (architecture, pre-training, fine-tuning, inference, prompting) and drills into two: using small (<=13B, even sub-1B) models and post-training quantization to 4-bit. She shows quantization cuts disk/memory and time-to-first-token with negligible quality loss at 4-bit but degradation at 3-bit, and stresses evaluating quantized models before deployment.

takeaways.technique: Prefer small fine-tuned models for narrow tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues small models (<=13B, even 350M-2B) after task-specific fine-tuning match much larger models on narrow tasks, so route narrow work to them.
takeaways.numbers: 3.8B model outperforms a ~7B model; 350M and 2B fine-tunes competitive on narrow tasks

takeaways.what_they_do: Reduce weight precision from 16/32-bit to 4-bit to cut memory, disk and latency with negligible quality loss; evaluate before deploying.
takeaways.evidence_quote: 4bit quantization was essentially free like we could just quantize with four bits
takeaways.numbers: 4-bit: negligible quality change, lower time-to-first-token; 3-bit: measurable drop

takeaways.technique: Evaluate quantized/cheaper models before swapping them in
takeaways.what_they_do: Run a standardized eval (text, trust/safety, vision) on the quantized model before deployment instead of assuming 4-bit is safe.
takeaways.evidence_quote: evaluating your quantize model is super important so don't just assume for bit is the answer

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat prompts as a latency and memory cost; keep them concise via template formatting and compression.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want your prompts to be as concise as possible concise as possible
